title: The Mountain of the Lord and the Day of the Lord
summary: Isaiah sees a future in which the mountain of the Lord's house is raised above all others and the nations stream to it to learn God's ways, and swords are beaten into plowshares. He then turns to Judah as it is: full of foreign practices, wealth, weapons, and idols. A day of the Lord is coming against everything proud and lofty, when people will throw away their idols and hide in the rocks, and the Lord alone will be exalted.
story: Chapter 1 put Judah on trial and promised that Jerusalem would be purified and called the Faithful City. Chapter 2 opens a new section (chapters 2 to 4) with its own heading and paints that restored Jerusalem on a world scale: not only Judah but all nations will come to Zion to be taught. Then, as Isaiah so often does, he sets the vision beside the present reality, and the contrast is sharp. The people who should be a light to the nations are instead copying them. The rest of the chapter announces the day of the Lord, a theme Amos had already used (Amos 5:18-20), when God will humble human pride. The section will end in chapter 4 with a cleansed Zion under God's protection.
historical:
The chapter reflects the prosperity of Judah in the eighth century BC, probably under Uzziah and Jotham, when the kingdom controlled trade routes, built fortifications, and accumulated wealth and military strength (2 Chronicles 26:6-15; 27:3-4). Verse 7's silver, gold, horses, and chariots are exactly what Deuteronomy 17:16-17 warned a king not to multiply. The influences from the east and the soothsaying like the Philistines point to foreign religious practices, especially divination, which came in along with trade and alliances.

Verses 2 to 4 appear almost word for word in Micah 4:1-3, and Micah adds a further line. Micah was Isaiah's younger contemporary in Judah. Scholars debate whether Isaiah borrowed from Micah, Micah from Isaiah, or both from an older song about Zion, and there is no certain answer. The cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan (verse 13) were the tallest and most prized trees of the region, and ships of Tarshish (verse 16) were large seagoing trading vessels, named after a distant port whose location is uncertain, often identified with a site in Spain.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, mountains were thought of as places where gods lived, and temples were often built on high places or designed as artificial mountains, like the ziggurats of Mesopotamia. Jerusalem's temple mount was not especially high, which makes the picture of it raised above all the hills a statement about God, not geography. The image of nations streaming to it reverses the story of Babel in Genesis 11, where people gathered to build a tower to make a name for themselves.

Swords and spears were costly iron weapons; plowshares and pruning hooks were farm tools made from the same metal. To beat one into the other was to turn the resources of war into the resources of food. The prophet Joel later reversed the image in a call to battle (Joel 3:10). Isaiah's line has had a long life outside Scripture: a bronze statue of a man beating a sword into a plowshare, given to the United Nations by the Soviet Union in 1959, stands in the garden of its New York headquarters. The idols Isaiah mocks were images of wood, stone, or metal, often overlaid with silver or gold, and worshipers bowed before them as the dwelling of a god.
literary: The chapter has two parts that sit side by side in deliberate tension. Verses 2 to 5 are a vision of the last days, ending with an invitation to the house of Jacob to walk in the Lord's light. Verses 6 to 22 are a poem of judgment built on repetition. Verse 9's line about mankind being brought low is repeated with variations in verses 11 and 17, and verses 10, 19, and 21 repeat the flight into the rocks from the terror of the Lord. Verses 12 to 16 are a list of ten lofty things, each introduced by against all, as though God were felling them one by one. The repeated refrain that the Lord alone will be exalted in that day is the chapter's center. It closes with a blunt proverb: stop trusting in man, whose life is only a breath.

outline.t: Heading: the word concerning Judah and Jerusalem
The nations stream to the mountain of the Lord
Come, walk in the light of the Lord
A land full of wealth, weapons, and idols
The day of the Lord against all that is proud
Idols thrown away as people flee

doctrines.note: Verses 2 to 4 picture God's reign reaching all nations, bringing instruction, justice, and peace. The kingdom is not Israel conquering the world but the world coming to learn from Israel's God.
The chapter links idolatry with pride, wealth, and military power. People bow to what their own hands have made, and on the day of the Lord they will throw those idols to the moles and bats.
The day of the Lord is aimed at pride: everything lofty, from trees to towers to ships, will be brought low. Judgment exposes what human beings have trusted instead of God.

words.note: Acharit, end or latter part, in the phrase the last days (verse 2). It can mean simply the future, the days to come, but prophets use it for the time when God will bring his purposes to completion. The New Testament writers believed those last days had begun with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2).

Torah, translated law in verse 3. Its basic meaning is instruction or teaching, the guidance a parent or priest gives, and by extension the teaching of Moses. The nations come to Zion not to be conquered but to be taught.
Elil, idol, used four times here. The word sounds like elohim, God, but likely means something weak or worthless. Isaiah uses it as a mocking term for the gods people make with their own fingers.

christ: The New Testament applies the language of the last days to the age that began with Jesus' resurrection and the pouring out of the Spirit (Acts 2:17). Christians have seen verses 2 to 4 beginning to be fulfilled as the word of the Lord went out from Jerusalem to the nations (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8), while the full end of war still awaits Christ's return. Jesus also taught that the proud will be humbled and the humble exalted (Luke 14:11), and the images of people hiding in the rocks from the terror of the Lord are echoed in Revelation 6:15-16 at the coming of the Lamb's wrath. How much of the vision is being fulfilled now in the church and how much awaits the end is debated among Christians, but all agree the peace it describes is the peace of Christ's kingdom.

hard.q: Should the vision of swords beaten into plowshares be read as a hope for this age or only for the age to come?
hard.a: Readers differ. Some Christians read the passage as describing the present spread of the gospel and see it partly fulfilled wherever Christ's rule reconciles enemies; they often draw from it an ethic of peacemaking now. Others, including many who expect a future earthly reign of Christ, read it as a promise for a coming age that cannot be realized by human effort. Jewish interpreters have long read it as a messianic hope still to come. Most agree on two points: that the passage makes peace flow from the nations learning God's ways, not from political arrangements alone, and that it shapes how God's people should live even before it is complete. Verse 5, with its invitation to the house of Jacob to walk in that light now, suggests the vision was meant to govern present conduct as well as future hope.

questions: Isaiah's people were wealthy and well armed, and their land was full of idols. What connection do you see between security, wealth, and idolatry?
What does it mean for you to walk in the light of the Lord (verse 5) before the world described in verses 2 to 4 has fully come?
Verse 22 tells us to stop trusting in man. Where are you most tempted to put your final trust in people or institutions?
